prompt:
Write 12 short claim log entries (one to three sentences each) by an auto insurance adjuster for a low-speed head-on collision claim, in time order. Injury: neck and back strain. The claimant is represented by a lawyer. Start each entry on a new line with 'Entry 1:', 'Entry 2:' and so on. No names, dates or amounts. (Internal reference C-1088; do not mention it.) Work these facts into the text naturally, in your own words, without listing them:
- The reported injury matches the kind and force of the crash well.
- Treatment grew to many times the usual amount for this injury, with near-daily visits and new body areas added weeks after the crash.
- No earlier injury to the same body area is known.
- Witnesses, photos and the other driver all confirm the accident happened as described.
- The vehicle damage matches the described impact.
- The claimant later added small details, but the account stayed the same.
- The police and witnesses confirm the claimant was in the vehicle.
- No earlier damage to the vehicle is known.
- Nothing suggests the damage happened before the coverage started.
- The driver is named on the policy.
text:
Entry 1: The claimant reported a low-speed head-on collision and stated that the policyholder's vehicle was struck while stopped in a lane. The claimant is now represented by an attorney, so all further contact will go through counsel.

Entry 2: Police confirmed the claimant was seated in the vehicle at the scene, and two independent witnesses have given statements consistent with the reported sequence of events. The other driver also described the collision the same way.

Entry 3: Scene photographs and the damage to the vehicle line up with the described impact. Nothing in the file suggests the damage predates the policy's effective date.

Entry 4: The driver is listed as a named insured on the policy, and the coverage was in force at the time of loss. No prior damage to the vehicle appears in our records or in the inspection report.

Entry 5: The claimant reported neck and back strain shortly after the collision, which fits the type and force of impact seen in the photographs. Medical records from the first visit describe pain consistent with that injury.

Entry 6: Initial treatment was modest, but over the following weeks the frequency of visits increased to nearly daily, and the volume of care is now well beyond what is usual for a strain of this kind. Pain was later reported in additional areas of the body that were not mentioned at the first visit.

Entry 7: Our search of prior claims and medical history found no earlier injury to the same areas of the neck and back. The claimant's prior records show no comparable complaints.

Entry 8: In a recorded follow-up, the claimant added some minor details about the position of the vehicles and the sequence of braking, but the core account has remained the same across every statement given so far.

Entry 9: Counsel has requested an evaluation of the claim and has asked that the carrier direct questions through the firm. I have acknowledged the request and noted the file accordingly.

Entry 10: I reviewed the treatment plan with the file and noted that the number of providers and the scope of therapy have expanded since the claim was opened. I have asked for the treating physician's rationale for the additional areas.

Entry 11: The claim file has been reviewed against the photographs, witness statements, police report, and vehicle inspection. The accounts agree with one another, and the physical evidence supports the reported impact.

Entry 12: Next steps include requesting the complete treatment records, confirming the physician's reasoning for the expanded care, and scheduling an independent medical review before any settlement discussion proceeds.
